The inert gas is a Ar-15%He mixture at a pressure of -10 inHg (or ~400 Torr), and prior to melting the alloys, a pure zirconium button is melted for ~1 minute in order to scavenge stray oxygen. Each button was melted six times, and the button was flipped between melts in order to get full component mixing. The operator uses the goals outlined below as a guide for determining how long to melt at each step and what aspects of the operation to focus upon. Typical individual melt times are >1 minute and <5 minutes. If needed, the operator may stop then re-strike and resume melting at any time; this may be necessary if the arc-melt chamber begins to overheat. A process log is kept for each button lot. • Melt 1- Incorporate all of the pieces into a single button and begin the alloying process without losing charge material though splattering or other events. • Melt 2 - Perform the alloying process by getting full melting and blending of the DU and alloying elements. Continue to melt until there are no longer any large (greater than 1/8”) pieces of charge visually observed floating on the button surface when it is molten. • Melt 3 - Complete alloying process; melt until there are no longer any pieces of alloying element visually observed floating on the button surface when it is molten (or visible on the bottom of the button when flipped over). • Melt >4 - Further melting steps should follow the same guidelines as that for "Melt 3" given above, but provide additional opportunities to identify and address any unmelted pieces. 24 Button melting can be a highly effective and accurate means of creating homogeneous samples of well-known compositions. The high temperature of the arc allows for easy melting of components, including refractory metals such as molybdenum, and the large Lorentz forces promote extremely fast mixing within the melt pool. The relatively inert conditions (water cooled metal components and inert gas atmosphere) minimize impurity sources and the relatively short total time in the liquid phase minimizes the time for reactions to occur. Repeated flipping of the button between melts minimizes the influence of either the solid skull/shell preventing complete mixing and the highly visible nature of the technique provides the operator with the ability to directly observe the condition of the melt. The preceding list of advantages does not imply that some caution is not warranted, and as such, the sources of potential error in sample compositions will be identified along side any mitigating actions taken for this study. High-grade uranium and molybdenum sources were used as charge for the buttons produced for this study. The uranium was of the depleted type (0.2 wt.% 235U); therefore, the molecular weight of the source uranium was estimated as 237.994 g/mol for all calculations. Since the exact daughter product concentrations evolve over time and can be altered by processing, no attempt was made to account for them separately in this study.
